parole.significato: Forms adjectives.
parole.testo: From Latin past participles in -ītus, of verbs in -īre, -ĕre, -ēre, partly via Old French.

parole.significato: To touch by means of a mutual border, edge or end; to border on; to lie adjacent (to); to be contiguous (said of an are…
parole.testo: From Middle English abutten, from Medieval Latin abuttare and Old French abuter, aboter, abouter (“to touch at one end, to come to an end, aim, reach”), from Old French but (“end, aim, purpose”); akin to Old Norse butr (“piece of wood”). Equivalent to a- (“to”) + butt (“boundary mark”).

parole.significato: The act of annunciating.
parole.testo: From Middle English annunciacion, annunciation, from Latin annuntiātiō and Old French anonciacion.

parole.significato: A senior administrative official in a diocese, just under the bishop, often in charge of an archdeaconry. As a title, i…
parole.testo: From Middle English arcedekne, archdecon, archdekne, archdekyn, archedeken, archedekyn, archedyacun, archideken, archidiacon, ardekne, ercedekene, ercedekne, erchdekene, erchedekene, erchedekne, erresdeken, ersedekne, ersedekyn, from Old English ærcedæcne, ærcediæcne, earcedæcne (from Late Latin arc

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Stachys.
parole.testo: From Middle English betayny, betanie, from Medieval Latin betōnia (possibly through Old French), from Latin betōnica or ve(t)tōnica, from Vettones, a people in Lusitania. Compare French bétoine.

parole.significato: Synonym of bordar (“person ranking below villeins and above serfs”).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin bordarius, from Old French borde (“hut, cabin, small farm”) + -arius.

parole.significato: A member of a Christian contemplative order of monks founded by Bruno of Cologne (St Bruno) in 1084.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin Carthusianus, from Cart(h)usia, Latinization of Old French Chartrouse, a region near Grenoble where the order was founded, now Chartreuse; from Late Latin Catorissium, Cantourisa, Caturissium, Chatrousse, probably ultimately from Gaulish *Katurīx (literally “battle-king”). Also s

parole.significato: A single-room dwelling for a hermit.
parole.testo: From Middle English celle, selle, from Old English cell (attested in inflected forms), from Latin cella (“chamber, small room, compartment”), later reinforced by Old French cel, sele, Old French cele. Ultimately from Proto-Italic *kelnā, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱelneh₂, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱ

parole.significato: Self-assurance.
parole.testo: From Middle English confidence, from Latin cōnfīdentia (possibly via Old French confidence), from cōnfīdō (“believe, confide in”) from con- (“with”) + fīdō (“trust”). By surface analysis, confide + ence.

parole.significato: Any of various metallic sulphates formed from the reaction of sulfur with iron, zinc, or copper, especially (alchemy) s…
parole.testo: From Middle English coperas, coperose (“any metallic sulfate”), from Medieval Latin cuprosa directly or via Old French coperose, from Medieval Latin aqua cuprosa (“cupreous water”), from Latin cuprum (“copper”) + -osa (“-ose: forming related adjectives”). Fanciful derivations from cupreous terms inv

parole.significato: The superintendent of the engravers of dies for making coins.
parole.testo: From cuneātor, Medieval Latin equivalent of Old French coigneur (“coiner”).

parole.significato: Small; diminutive.
parole.testo: From Middle English diminute, from Latin dīminūtus and Old French diminut.

parole.significato: Donor, one who donates.
parole.testo: From Middle English donatour, from Latin dōnātor and Old French; equivalent to donate + -or.

parole.significato: A proclamation of law or other authoritative command.
parole.testo: From Middle English edycte, borrowed from Latin edictum; earlier form edit, from Old French edit, from the same Latin word.

parole.significato: The full profits or products yielded by land, such as hay, pasturage, grain, rents, services, and the like.
parole.testo: From Latin expletia, Old French espleit. Compare exploit.

parole.significato: A band or cap (usually metal) placed around a shaft to reinforce it or to prevent splitting.
parole.testo: From Middle English verel, virel, virole (“ferrule; metal pivot on the end of an axle”), altered under the influence of Latin ferrum (“iron”), from Old French virole (“ferrule”), from Latin viriola (“little bracelet”), diminutive of viria (“bracelet worn by men”), from Gaulish, from Proto-Celtic *we

parole.significato: Synonym of Franciscan: a member of the Order of the Friars Minor.
parole.testo: A calque of Medieval Latin Fratres Minores (“the Lesser Brothers”), both directly and via Old French freres meneurs and Norman freres menures, a name supposedly chosen by St Francis to inculcate humility.

parole.significato: The physiological faculty of taste.
parole.testo: From Middle English gust, guste, from Latin gustus (“taste”) and Old French gust, goust.

parole.significato: The sweet and edible drupes (fruits) of several Mediterranean and African species of small trees.
parole.testo: From Middle English jujube, from Medieval Latin jujuba or Old French jujube, perhaps via Old Occitan from Classical Latin zīzyphum, zīzyphus, from Ancient Greek ζίζυφον (zízuphon)․ First attested in the 14th century.

parole.significato: Anything made of wool, or woolworking.
parole.testo: From Latin lanificium: compare Old French lanifice.

parole.significato: A person native to ancient Rome or its Empire.
parole.testo: From Middle English Latin, Latyn, from Old English Lǣden, from Vulgar Latin *ladinum (“Latin”) and Old French latin (“Latin”); all from Latin Latinus (“belonging to Latium”). Later influenced in form by the Latin word. Compare Dutch Latijn (“Latin”), German Latein (“Latin”), Swedish Latin (“Latin”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to praise, or the expression of praise.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin laudatōrius: compare Old French laudatoire.

parole.significato: Slowness; sluggishness.
parole.testo: From Latin lentitūdo, from lentus (“slow”). Compare Old French lentitude.

parole.significato: From or in a nearby location.
parole.testo: From Middle English local, from Late Latin locālis (“belonging to a place”), possibly also via Old French local; ultimately from Latin locus (“a place”). parole.significato: To furnish with machicolations.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin machicolātus, perfect participle of machicolāre, from Old French machicoller, from machicolleis (“machicolation”), from Old Occitan machacol, from macar (“to crush”) + col (“neck”).

parole.significato: An opening between corbels that support a projecting parapet, or in the floor of a gallery or the roof of a portal, of…
parole.testo: From Late Latin machicol(amentum) (“machicolation”) + -ation (suffix indicating an action or process). Machicolamentum may be derived from Old French macher (“to chew; to crush”) (modern French mâcher) + col (“neck”) + Latin -mentum (suffix indicating an instrument or medium, or the result of someth

parole.significato: The edge of the paper, typically left blank when printing but sometimes used for annotations etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English margyn, from Latin marginem (possibly via Old French margin), accusative of margō (“edge, brink, border, margin”). Doublet of marge and margo.

parole.significato: Mass; a church service.
parole.testo: From Middle English mes, partly from Old English mēse, mēose (“table”), a vernacular loan from Latin/Late Latin mē(n)sa (“table; meal”); and partly from Old French mes, Late Latin missum, from mittō (“to put, place (e.g. on the table)”). See mission, and compare Mass (“religious service”).

parole.significato: A mining business.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin mineria, minaria, from Old French miniere.

parole.significato: A dull or stupid person.
parole.testo: Ultimately from the name of Momus, god of mirth, through Latin and Old French.

parole.significato: The Church regarded as nourishing and protecting its members.
parole.testo: From an association of spiritual comfort and hierarchy with familial relationships, probably originally as a calque of similar expressions in other languages, especially 2nd-century Latin mater ecclesia (“mother church”) and 12th-century Old French mere eglise (“mother church”).

parole.significato: Any alteration or change.
parole.testo: Late 14th century as Middle English mutacioun, from Latin mūtātiō, both directly and via Old French mutacion.

parole.significato: Occurring or appearing irregularly from time to time, but not often; incidental.
parole.testo: From Middle English occasyonal, from Medieval Latin occāsiōnālis and Old French ocasionel. By surface analysis, occasion + -al.

parole.significato: Synonym of ophthalmitis (“inflammation of the eye”).
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin obtalmia and Old French obtalmie, ultimately from Ancient Greek ὀφθαλμός (ophthalmós). Re-classicized from the Greek spelling, instead of archaic obtalmy (“eye inflammation, (also?) longsightedness”).

parole.significato: Something which is packed, a parcel, a box, an envelope.
parole.testo: Equivalent to pack + -age. Possibly influenced by Anglo-Latin paccagium or Old French pacquage.

parole.significato: The highest form of bishop, in the ancient world having authority over other bishops in the province but now generally…
parole.testo: From Middle English patriark, patriarche, from Late Latin patriarcha; later reinforced by Old French patriarche, from Ancient Greek πατριάρχης (patriárkhēs, “the founder of the tribe/family”), from Ancient Greek πατριά (patriá, “generation, ancestry, descent, tribe, family”) + -ᾰ́ρχης (-ắrkhēs, “-ar

parole.significato: An entryway or gate.
parole.testo: Inherited from the Old English port, from the Latin porta (“passage, gate”), reinforced by the Old French porte. Doublet of porta.

parole.significato: Something prescribed; a rule, regulation or dictate.
parole.testo: Latin praescriptum: compare Old French prescript.

parole.significato: An instance of applying pressure; an instance of pressing.
parole.testo: From Middle English presse (“throng, crowd, clothespress”), partially from Old English press (“clothespress”) (from Medieval Latin pressa) and from Old French presse (Modern French presse) from Old French presser (“to press”), from Latin pressāre, from pressus, past participle of premere (“to press”

parole.significato: A nun in charge of a priory (usually lower in rank than an abbess); mother superior.
parole.testo: From Middle English prieresse, priorasse, priores, prioresse, priorisse, priouresse, priures, priuresse, prowres, pryoras, pryorys, pryowresse, from Medieval Latin priōrissa and Old French prioresse, prieuresse; equivalent to prior + -ess.

parole.significato: A site for mining stone, such as limestone, or slate.
parole.testo: From Middle English quarere, from Medieval Latin quarreria (1266), literally a “place where stones are squared”, from Old French quarrière (compare modern French carrière), from Vulgar Latin *quadraria, from Latin quadrō (“to square”), itself from quadra (“a square”), from quattuor (“four”), ultimat

parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English rabet, rabette, from Anglo-Latin rabettus, from dialectal Old French rabotte, probably a diminutive of Middle Dutch or West Flemish robbe (“rabbit, seal”), of uncertain origin; possibly some imitative verb, maybe robben, rubben (“to rub”) is used here to allude to a cha

parole.significato: recoverable
parole.testo: From Middle English recuperable, from Medieval Latin recuperābilis and Old French recuperable. By surface analysis, recuperate + -able.

parole.significato: Senses relating to placing or positioning.
parole.testo: From Middle English reposen (“to put (something) back, replace”), from re- (prefix meaning ‘again; back, backwards’) + posen (“to place (something)”), modelled after Latin repōnō (“to put back; to restore; to store”). Posen is derived from Old French poser (“to place, put”) (modern French poser), fr

parole.significato: residence; abode
parole.testo: Latin reseantia, Old French reseance.

parole.significato: Any of several Mediterranean herbs, of the genus Satureja, grown as culinary flavourings.
parole.testo: From Middle English saverey, possibly from Old English sæþerie, from Latin satureia, influenced by or via Old French savereie.

parole.significato: The north or northern regions.
parole.testo: From Middle English septentrion, septentrione, septemtryones, septemtrioun, from Latin septentriō, septentriōnem (“the northern regions, the north”) directly and through Old French septentrïon, septemtrion, from septentriōnēs (“the seven stars near the north pole”) (called Charles's Wain, or the Gre

parole.significato: A fine thin linen muslin or cambric cloth.
parole.testo: From Latin sindōn (possibly by way of Old French syndone and sindone), from Ancient Greek σινδών (sindṓn), from Late Egyptian šndy(t), from earlier šnḏwt (“kilt”).

parole.significato: Miscellaneous items or objects; (with possessive) personal effects.
parole.testo: From Middle English stuf, stuffe, from Anglo-Latin stuffa and its etymon Old French estofe, estoffe, estuf, estuffe, stoffe, from estoffer, estofer (“to provide what is necessary, equip, stuff”), borrowed from Old High German stoffōn, from Proto-West Germanic *stoppōn (“to clog up, block, fill”). Mo

parole.significato: A specific pitch.
parole.testo: From Middle English ton, tone, from Latin tonus (“sound, tone”) (possibly through Old French ton), from Ancient Greek τόνος (tónos, “strain, tension, pitch”), from τείνω (teínō, “to stretch”). Doublet of tune, ton, tonos, and tonus.

parole.significato: A set of 30 requiem masses, said once a day for a month or all in one day.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin trentāle directly or via Old French trentel, from the neuter substantive of *Vulgar Latin trenta + -ālis (“-al: forming adjectives”), from Latin trīgintā (“thirty”).

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or being a triumph.
parole.testo: From Middle English triumphal, triumphall, tryumphal, from Latin triumphālis and Old French trionfal, triumphal.

parole.significato: A word that indicates an action, event, or state of being.
parole.testo: From Middle English verbe, directly from Latin verbum (“word, verb”), reinforced by Old French verbe, from Proto-Indo-European *werdʰo-. Doublet of verve and word.
